name: Navigate or redirect the tab
plain: Sends the current tab to a different page by script, meta refresh or server redirect.
meaning: A site can move the person to another URL at any time, including after they click something. Cross-origin iframes get tighter limits, which is why ad frames cannot hijack the whole tab.

web.api: location.href / assign() / replace(); <meta http-equiv=refresh>; HTTP 301/302/303/307/308; top.location from an iframe

access.revocation: Nothing to revoke (no permission is stored)
access.iframe: Cross-origin iframe may navigate top only with user activation (sandbox allow-top-navigation-by-user-activation) or allow-top-navigation
steps: Script runs location.assign or sets location.href
beforeunload may ask the person to stay

limits.headline: Can send your current tab to another page by itself
limits.user_action: Nothing. It happens on load, after a timer, or when you submit a form.
can: Send you to a new page after a login, a payment or a link
Move you from an old address to a new one
Open a different page in the same tab through a redirect
cannot: Send you away from a page you never opened, such as a page inside someone else's frame, in most browsers
Skip the browser's warning for a risky site
Stop you using Back; the earlier page stays in history
limits.reach_label: The tab it is running in
limits.differs: Chrome, Safari and Firefox all stop most hidden redirects from embedded frames, but how strict they are differs.

story.what_it_is: A page can send your tab to a different address by script, redirect or timer.
story.for_you: Most of the time you click a link and arrive. Sometimes you land on a different page than you clicked, for example after a login or a shortened link.
story.for_makers: Redirects are the plumbing of the web: login flows, short links, regional sites. They also power click tracking, because the hop through an ad server lets it count the click.

use_cases.example: A tap on an ad goes through a tracking server that counts the click, then forwards you to the advertiser.
You are sent to your bank, then to an identity page, then back with a signed in session.
A phishing mail link bounces you through several sites to hide the real destination.
A short link from a message expands into a long product URL with a discount code.
A browser game portal redirects you to the game's own site on a different domain.
A booking site sends you to a payment partner and then back to confirm your trip.

technical_bounds: Same-frame navigation needs no activation or prompt
Cross-origin iframe navigating the top frame is blocked without user activation (Chrome 64 framebusting intervention; sandboxed frames need allow-top-navigation*)
Navigating to data: or blob: URLs in the top frame by script is blocked in Chrome 60 and Firefox 59 for data:
Browsers cap redirect chains (Chrome and Firefox stop after 20 redirects)
Navigations flooded in a loop are throttled (Chrome IPC flooding protection, Safari 100 per 30 s)

abuse: Redirect chains used for bounce tracking

history.change: Cross-origin iframe redirects of the top frame need user activation
Block renderer-initiated top-level navigation to data: URLs

refs.label: Chrome: Prevent unwanted redirects from iframes
